utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. If you could be seated. Mr. Djurdjic continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. Sir, we did tab 52 yesterday, that was the last thing we did, right? General, sir, what I'd like to know is this: In 1999 during the Kosovo Verification Mission operation in Kosovo and Metohija, did you know anything, or did you do anything about their dealings with certain Albanians whose activities were at the time targeting the VJ and generally speaking the security forces of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went through a number of documents yesterday showing that we knew that the Kosovo Verification Mission in Kosovo and Metohija which was established following the signing of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement was monitoring all of the army and MUP activity, but they were also supposed to monitor any activities by the KLA terrorists. We knew that the mission sometimes exceeded its mandate. They were sometimes in contact with certain citizens and they sometimes visited some terrorist HQ. They would give away information regarding the location, activities, and manpower of the VJ and MUP in Kosovo and Metohija. I believe that definitely exceeded their mandate, what they were there for. In addition to that we had information indicating in two particular cases, or rather, two particular cases where we managed to actually document the fact that some members of the Kosovo Verification Mission made an effort to win over some Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija in terms of getting them to do intelligence work for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember the case of Bekim Kastrati could you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do remember that. He was an ex-colonel of the VJ or rather, ex-sergeant of the VJ. Sometime early 1998 he led the ranks of the VJ and got a job with the Kosovo Verification Mission at their Pristina HQ. We managed to obtain some intelligence indicating that he was in touch with certain members of the Kosovo Verification Mission, and at a certain point in time, he was, in fact, gathering intelligence on the activities of certain army units, VJ army units and MUP units regarding potential NATO targets and regarding the effects of NATO air-strikes. We tried to put a stop to this activity on his part. He was, in fact, working with another three Albanians. As soon as early January 1999, there was a meeting where he met with two US officers who were members of the OSCE Mission in Kosovo and Metohija. He received assignments at that meeting, and he was told on how to keep them informed about any movements by the VJ and the MUP. He was also to keep them up to date on the effects of NATO air-strikes on certain targets in the general Pristina area. For that purpose, he was given a mobile telephone. Following the withdrawal of the Kosovo Verification Mission, he was given a satphone as well. He was actually recorded using that phone in order to get in touch with these two officer to submit reports to them. This was after the Kosovo Verification Mission had left Kosovo already, and by this time they were stationed in Skopje, Macedonia. In order to prevent him from doing that, from continuing to do that, we arrested and prosecuted Mr. Kastrati. During the actual trial, he admitted to these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to tab 53 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also have D011-3392. I'd like to that see that on our screens. That's 1805, Your Honours. That's the Defence document number. Your Honours, the Defence moves that the exhibit be added to our 65 ter list, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems no opposition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number is D011-3342.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are told it is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We might have got the numbers wrong, but I believe Ms. O'Leary will be able to track down the right number. 3342. I may have misread 3342. 011-3342.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a sentence passed by the military court attached to the military district command in Pristina, the 8th of April, 1999. The sentenced person is Bekim Kastrati. Does this sentence concern the activities that you discussed a while ago on the part of Bekim Kastrati? Was he eventually convicted?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me one thing. Do you remember exactly when you arrested Bekim Kastrati?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was arrested, I believe, on the 13th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document please be exhibited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00769.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have Exhibit P946.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 54 for you, sir. This is a combat report by the Pristina Corps Command, the date is the 4th of April, 1999. It was dispatched to the 3rd Army Command. General, sir, I would like to know more about paragraph 5, if you could please shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 5 of this report informs the superior command by the fact that as of the 4th of April, 1999, mixed check-points started work throughout Kosovo and Metohija of the Ministry of the Interior and the VJ. These check-points were set up along access roads to major townships and cities in order to check any passing civilian traffic in the case of the Ministry of the Interior as well as any passing military traffic in the case of the VJ. The paragraph also states how many criminal reports were filed for offences committed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were all persons checked as well as all vehicles passing these check-points?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, did you have any knowledge about ethnic Albanians leaving the area early 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The departure of ethnic Albanians throughout 1998, I would say, was a wide-spread phenomenon. Albanians from rural environments tended to move to towns, major towns partly in a bit to avoid forcible mobilisation and partly because they were driven out by some KLA activities, partly also because there had been some operations by the security forces during which there was firing from their homes and houses. Those were damaged as a result. In 1998 I had the impression that the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija tended to group more and more in urban centres and towns. Sometime late in February and early in March that year, it was becoming clearer and clearer that there would be NATO air-strikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Particularly in late March and early April 1999 there was a mass movement of the Albanian population. They were leaving Kosovo and Metohija en masse, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: According to your information what were the reasons for that trend?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was quite difficult. More than other areas throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Kosovo and Metohija, was being subjected to daily strikes by NATO and nightly strikes, if I may put it that way. One of the reasons was certainly the fear felt by the population. They were fearing the effects of NATO air-strikes. Another reason would be the fact that in Pristina, for example, where my own security section was located, although supplied to other towns too, living conditions were quite miserable for the population. I also know that the transformer station was targeted by air-strikes in Pristina, therefore, there was no electricity. The waterworks building was targeted as well. This continued throughout, almost up until the end of April. There was a thick plume of smoke above Pristina all the time because the oil derivative warehouse, a major one, was also targeted near the Serb cemetery in Pristina. The post office building was targeted too. Many people from Kosovo and Metohija were working abroad somewhere in the EU, and they were unable to get in touch with their relatives in Kosovo and Metohija. Another thing was rumours were circulating as well as a good deal of misinformation. There was talk indicating that Chetniks would come in from the part of Kosovo neighbouring on Serbia. Leaflets were being dropped by planes all over the place. There was a lot of misinformation around. Nevertheless, the one fundamental reason for this trend was the actual fear that people felt. They were afraid in terms of their own physical safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the members of the other ethnicities in Kosovo, were they leaving too?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since the start of NATO air-strikes those primarily who could muster the courage to actually cross the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the Serbs were moving back to Serbia, the Albanians were moving further south towards Macedonia and the Republic of Albania. In actual fact all those who had a place to go tried to leave Kosovo and Metohija and find refuge elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the military aspect? Was it convenient that all these people were leaving Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered this question already while testifying in the Milutinovic trial. As for us soldiers, as for any soldier possessing any military knowledge at all, no matter how modest, one thing was absolutely clear. Our units and our positions were prepared to face an enemy landing, and the best thing for us would have been to keep the area as densely inhabited as possible, the reason being NATO's aviation would have had a much harder time identifying potential targets and selecting targets for their air-strikes. We had no doubt about one thing at the Pristina Corps HQ. People leaving was a very unfavourable trend for us, very undesirable. We tried to use the local authorities to influence these trends and to keep people from leaving. We knew that as soon as we were alone, left alone in Kosovo and Metohija, anything would easily have become a potentially military target as well as easy prey for NATO's aviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of the existence of a plan to forcefully move the Albanian population out of Kosovo and Metohija in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of the existence of such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have any operative information about the VJ and members of the Ministry of the Interior encouraging people to move out or instigating such migration in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning any members of the MUP, I did not have information to that extent. As for the Army of Yugoslavia, I'm certain that it was not trying to force the population move out of Kosovo and Metohija by any of its measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Had any MUP members undertaken such measures, would you have received information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had any members of the MUP, given that Pristina is a large town tried to do something of the sort, I would have received at least some information from my subordinate security organs as well as from ordinary citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any calls to put a halt to the people moving out of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the political level, there was a number of talks with representatives of moderate Albanian political parties. I also know that the staff of the Supreme Command in April, I believe, put out a proclamation. They tried to have it printed in the Albanian news, primarily in "Koha Ditore" but in other Albanian papers as well. It was served -- it would serve to make clear to the Albanian population that they should not leave their homes and that they are safe where they are, and that they should stay in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This document, is that a document on the screen, are you wanting to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, certainly. It will -- it's already an exhibit we are told. P946. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. It has taken us so long that I've forgotten which exhibit I wanted to have. Now we have D180.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is this the proclamation you referred to? It is your tab 55.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see in the stamp that it says the General Staff of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, could we please have D006-2505.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 56. This is a report of the security section of the 3rd Army Command dated 13 April 1999 sent to the Supreme Command staff, its security administration. And item 1, General, it says that members of the Pristina Corps in the area of the village of Ajnovci killed terrorists Nazmi Milaku and Aslan Sopi. Did you notify the 3rd Army Command security department of this, or did this information originally come from you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the role of these two arrested terrorists, and please comment on item 3 of this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two terrorists were in the area of Novo Brdo. This is where they were arrested, having previously participated in a number of crimes about which they gave statements. In item 3 it is stated that Mr. Sopi was witness to 20 Serb civilians in December 1998 when there was a cease-fire and while the OSCE Mission was in Kosovo. Those 20 civilians were killed by Siptar terrorists. He also states that in the village of Bradas five Serbs were killed. This is but a portion of their statement which is much much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we go to item 5 next, please. Just a moment, let us see it on the screen first.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carrying out their functional duties, the security organs of the Pristina Corps in very difficult and almost unbearable circumstances strove to perform those duties as best they could, which is why they frequently encountered obstacles. Before commenting item 4, I will mention only a few such obstacles. In the performance of his duties, the chief of security of the 549th Motorised Brigade was killed, Captain 1st Class Dragan Mikicevic. He was killed by Siptar terrorists in the area of Orahovac. In the performance of his duties, the chief of security of the tactical group 252, Major Vojin Lukic was killed by Siptar terrorists in the area of Lipljani. In the performance of his duties during on-site investigation in the area of Volujak along the road between Klina and Djakovica, NATO airplane struck his armed personnel carrier killing Lieutenant Milic and his four soldiers. Another team was moving to carry out an on-site investigation along the road between Pristina and Pec. Their armoured personnel carrier was killed having come across a mine planted by terrorists. The whole crew was killed. We saw yesterday in an exhibit that there was mention made of a vehicle with eight members of the military police being kidnapped. In item 5 it is stated that in the process of bringing in two conscripts who had committed a criminal offence from Prizren to Pristina in the area of the Dulje pass, VJ members were kidnapped by the KLA. The two conscripts, a reserve captain, a driver, and the member of the military police from the 549th Brigade were all kidnapped. They are still considered missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00770.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-3191.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 58. Here we see the security department of the 3rd Army Command forwarding a document on the 16th of April to the Supreme Command staff concerning the statements of Nazmi Milaku and Aslan Sopi. Could you please comment page 3 of the English. We see part of the statement of Milaku Nazmi. I'm interested in the end of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these two Albanian terrorists, after an interview was conducted with them, were taken to the military investigative prison following the orders of the chief of security in Nis. Their interrogation was resumed there. These statements came about as a result of those interrogations. Milaku Nazmi, among other things in this statement, says that in the action Dolac, Dobre Vode, Stepenice, Iglarevo and so on, he personally killed three army members and wounded two MUP members. Also he stated that they suffered greater losses. He also says we, meaning terrorist staffs, were often visited by humanitarian organisations which brought us foodstuffs and medication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 6 in the English, which is part of the statement of Aslan Sopi. It is your page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph is what I'm interested in where it says, "in addition to that type of assistance."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the second paragraph, Aslan Sopi, the arrested terrorist, stated that: "We received monetary and other types of aid from your compatriots employed abroad, and in particular, we received aid and food and medicaments from international humanitarian organisations. We also received assistance from two members of the KVM, two Germans, and a Frenchman who was 40 years old. They came almost every day and sometimes twice a day to see Remi, that is Mustafa Rustemi aka Remi commander of the KLA Lab operational zone." He goes on to say, And gave him information. Remi's interpreter was from Podujevo and spoke German and English. What is particularly surprising is something that occurs in this last paragraph. It says: "In addition to the information already mentioned, the three OSCE members, immediately prior to the OSCE Mission departure from Kosovo, brought military maps with the exact locations of VJ and MUP units positions in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These statements were provided to the members of the military police. It's 52nd Battalion in Pristina. Thank you very.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00771.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D006-3298.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 57, Defence document 137. This is a report of the 14th Counter-intelligence Group dated 15 April, 1999. Please have a look at the third paragraph from the bottom. I believe it is the second page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the third paragraph from the top, it says that KLA terrorist staffs regrouped and adjusted their actions to the conditions under NATO air-strikes whereby they joined the operational zones of Salja and Lab. It covered the general area of Podujevo up to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terrorists are faced with shortages of food --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It says Salja and Lab. According to the latest information, that's the paragraph. What does it say in the rest of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called special unit comprising of 150 terrorists is active against the VJ and the MUP from this formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the rest of the sentence in addition to the joining of two zones?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrorists are facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Those forcefully mobilising the remaining Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what was your information at the time concerning the treatment of Albanian civilians by the KLA who were in refugee groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of the villages that were not effected by combat activities in 1998 and early 1999, their inhabitants did not move to larger towns. For that reason, they were facing a shortage of manpower. For that reason, the terrorists were exerting pressure throughout that period in a bid to mobilise all able-bodied men to fight with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00772.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-3312, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 59 for you, sir. Defence Exhibit number 141. Rather Defence document number 141. Just a minute, please, we'd like to have that on our screens first. Could you please comment on paragraph 1 of this document. It's a telegram, I believe, or a letter sent by the 3rd Army Command security department to the Supreme Command staff. Paragraph 1, please, if you could focus on that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 focuses on the case of four soldiers belonging to the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of the anti-aircraft defence. They have their HQ, their command at Djakovica, and some of their units were in Crmljan village. This is a case that was documented by the military police security organs. Some persons were also prosecuted. These four soldiers attempted to rape four Albanian women. During the war when it came to the units of the VJ we had a total of three cases of rape and two cases of attempted rape. I can give you the exact locations. Nevertheless, all of the persons involved were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00773.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D010-0163, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tab 60 for you, sir. As we see, it's a telegram by the Pristina Corps Command dated the 22nd of April, 1998 dispatched to the 3rd Army Command. Could you please explain what this is about? What sort of activities is it that we are looking at here and focus on paragraph 1 of this telegram first.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just set the record straight. This is no telegram. This is a report produced by the units for electronic surveillance and disruption. This was submitted to the Pristina Corps Command on a daily basis and also to the competent bodies or authorities within the 3rd Army. This is a journalist report indicating that the Serb forces around the village of Babaloc were trying to take control of a hill-top in order to be able to exercise control over the entire area. Nevertheless, they were being hampered in their attempt. They don't have any statements or declarations made by any of the Serb officials. They don't know what is being done politically about this. Nevertheless, they got a statement from the KLA which they believe was sufficient for their purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please just explain on the left-hand side, I'm looking at the bottom the document, technically speaking is this a telegram or what?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically speaking, yes, it's a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D00774, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter OTP document 5056.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is tab 61, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. 65 ter 4056. 4056.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's an Official Note by the security organ, Major Miroslav Babic in this case, the 27th of April, 1999. Sir, could you please comment on paragraph 3 of this Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an Official Note of the chief of security of the 175th Infantry Brigade. It was deployed in the general area surrounding this check-point described here in the village of Klokot. As I mentioned awhile ago, this is along the axis roads to Gnjilane and Vitina. We had mixed check-points along the axis roads to major towns. He is here describing the work of this mixed check-point set up along this road and manned by VJ and MUP members. There were some problems there because the municipality authority and some of the MUP bodies were adamant that the check-point should be removed since it was easy to spot from a plane and was certain to be targeted. The Official Note in paragraph 4 goes on to describe how the check-points operated. Two unidentified persons in camouflage uniform broke into the home of an Albanian village of Podujevo. They tried to loot the house and then the MPs from the check-points stepped in with some MUP organs. They used the daughter of that Albanian as a human shield, took her as far as the garden fence and then took her elsewhere, nobody knew where. It also states that two military conscripts from that brigade broke into the home of two old Serb ladies. They seised some items there as well as weapons and money. The military police from that check-point arrested these two. The items were seised back from them and handed over to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00775.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-3303.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We have here a report by the 3rd Army security department, 2nd of May, 1995. This is addressed to the Supreme Command staff, specifically their security administration. But I'm looking at paragraph 12 here, if you could focus on that, sir, please, and comment. This is page 5 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary report that was drafted by the security department of the 3rd Army on a daily basis. They were under an obligation to submit this on a daily basis to the security administration of the Supreme Command staff. Paragraph 12 is the last paragraph. It provides an overview in relation to two days, the 1st and 2nd of May, 1999. The security organs of the military police filed a total of 48 criminal reports to the relevant authorities and the prosecutors. They are here listing categories of persons and the type of criminal offence involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00776.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D006-3204. Tab 63. Defence document number 124. Thank you. Page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Page 2 for you, sir, as well. We have electronic operations here, paragraph 2. Did you know anything more about this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, they are analysing the results of electronic surveillance work. Among other things they obtained intelligence based on intercepted conversation between a member of the Albanian terrorist groups and a collocutor. They learned that they had some Serbs whom they captured, and these were now being kept in the Republic of Albania. The reference is probably here to those Serbs who had been kidnapped earlier on in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's move on to page 6 of the English. In your document that is page 4, sir. It reads: "Over the last 24 hours the information centre had received a total of 197 calls."

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where was this information centre, and what exactly did they do? What sort of activities? We see that this is as late as the 5th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information centre that was attached to the Pristina Corps Command. Throughout the war, it kept operating, and it was, in fact, operating in the basement of the Grand Hotel in Pristina. They had several computers there where they kept records of all members of the Pristina Corps in terms of the units that they belonged to and their location at the time. The information centre released information both to the media and the press. There was a media centre in the hotel itself. The hotel continued to operate throughout the war. They were up on one of the upper floors, and the information centre was in the basement in what used to be a pool billiard room. It was from there that they would normally release information to people such as parents who wanted to know about the fate of their children who were at the time members of the Pristina corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very. In addition to the information centre at the grand hotel, did the corps also have other components relevant to its command stationed there during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: The document that I'm seeing on the screen did not seem to be what they were just talking about. I don't know if I have the wrong -- if we are talking about a different exhibit or if anyone else is having the same concern. I didn't see anything about an information centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mine is dealing a lot with boots and underwear, Mr. Djurdjic. You may have the wrong page or the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope only the page is wrong. D, when I see that, that is quite correct. Persons killed. But let me check this again. Could we please have page 1 back on our screens because that's the easiest way to check the B/C/S, please. It should be the 5th of June, 1999, which it is. Thank you very much. Now let's move on to page 6 of the English. I think it's the first paragraph on that page, on page 6 in the English document. Page 6, and the paragraph number is number 4 towards the bottom, towards the end of paragraph 4, it reads, "over the last 24 hours," but that appears to be on the next page. There you go. "During the past 24 hours ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, what I should ask you is this: This is an information centre. This is the information centre at the Pristina Corps. Did all the elements of the Pristina Corps Command have external security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the regulations then in force, the relevant regulations, any element in the combat disposition of the Pristina Corps Command would have enjoyed protection measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me who was in the security detail protecting this information centre of the Pristina Corps during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only talking about command elements, specifically the command elements of the Pristina Corps. Those were secured by members of the military police, meaning members of the 52nd Battalion of the military police in the present case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever go to that information centre during the war in 1999? If so, what were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went there several times. My officers from the section went there too. One of the reasons being that was where we were receiving all of our mail from our superior command. They went there to pick up the mail in order to forward it to the appropriate commands. I went there to ask questions about certain members of the police battalion. My clerks went there to seek information about certain persons who were subject to criminal proceedings. We didn't know which unit to find them in because the units kept shifting in terms of their location and also the makeup of these units was not permanent. It was changing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00777.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D008-6914.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 64. Just a moment, we still don't have it. It is the security section of the 3rd Army Command, the 21st of June, 1999 sent to the security administration. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from the security section on the 21st of June, sent to the Supreme Command staff and its security administration following our work. Security organs of the Pristina Corps concerning all the information they had about the commission of a crime, always lodged a criminal report. In 1998, we submitted 1.570 criminal reports against members of the Pristina Corps and its resubordinated units for different types of crime. During the 78 days of bombardment between the 24th of March and the 10th of June, we submitted 246 criminal reports. 78 days is a short time to shed light on a crime. Therefore, many investigative activities were resumed after the NATO aggression, after which the territorial competent courts took over those cases. This concerns a terrible crime committed by a member of the 37th Motorised Brigade by the name of Stefan Jekic, a military conscript, while commanding a volunteer platoon ordered to his soldiers to place a civilian on a meadow following which they forced him to run, and they exercised their shooting on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What does it mean "a volunteer platoon"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the units of the Pristina Corps there were volunteers who had arrived through the collection centre in Belgrade in Gradska [phoen] Street and another section in the village of Medjak near Leskovac having passed security checks and certain training. Such people were then sent to the different units of the Pristina Corps. The command of the Pristina Corps, I know that very well, was against any volunteers being received from the outset. However, it was the position of the superior command that this should go on because people should not be prevented from defending their homeland. We all know what sort of trouble volunteers can bring. It is for that reason that the command of the Pristina Corps ordered its subordinate commanders to disperse all volunteers arriving in their unit across all of their subordinate units so as not to allow any greater concentration of volunteers in a single unit. This is a volunteer platoon of such nature from the 137th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you this: If a person, who has war time deployment duty, moves to a theatre, can such a person be a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, such a person cannot be considered a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00778.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: To illustrate this further, we'll show a few documents concerning the resumption of your work after the cessation of hostilities. You continued prosecuting the perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that reason, I would kindly ask to be shown document D008-4512. Sorry, D008-4152.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The document is dated the 25th of June. Supplemental report of the security organs of the 3rd Army Command.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can recall, this is concerning Rados Avramovic, military conscript from the 37th Motorised Brigade. There was a refugee column in the area of Drenica in the village near Glogovac. He singled out an Albanian woman and raped her. Subsequently he fled, but according to the information I had, he was found shortly afterwards and prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00779.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D008-4155. It is also a document of the 25th of June, 1999 from the 3rd Army. Another supplement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something more about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another example of a terrible crime. The report is about three military conscripts from the 27th Motorised Brigade. I think it was the village of Cirez although I'm not sure because a lot of time has passed. They tied an Albanian to a tractor there, killed him, and then burned him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00780.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D008-4160.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The same type of document from the security section of the 3rd Army dated the 9th of July. Can you tell us anything about that? It is your tab 68.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document there is information which came from the security organ of the Pristina Corps. It has to do with a crime committed by a group of volunteers from the 185th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: 175th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Infantry Brigade in the area of the village of Prilepnica and the village of Mucibaba in the Gnjilane municipality. The group was headed by Vlado Zmajevic. The entire case file was processed. This group of volunteers as well as another group of volunteers from the same brigade, headed by Vlado Zmajevic committed a number of crimes as well in the village of Zegra near Gnjilane. All these volunteers were first driven out of Kosovo and Metohija, and next we conducted a complete investigation. Once we had sufficient evidence, we issued arrest warrants, all of them were arrested, prosecuted, and convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00781.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djurdjic, or do you prefer to go until quarter to?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Or we can take the break as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will continue, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll agree with having a break if you desire so, but I can go on as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, we will continue. I thought you were indicating you needed a break, but we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have MFI D210.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is an information note of the security department of the 3rd Army Command dated the 13th of May, 1999. Does this correspond to what you know about how reports were drafted by the security administration?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The information contained therein, did any of that information come from your security section of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no information which it come from the security section of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the crime which took place in Podujevo, do you know whether there were any prosecutions launched against anyone?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This event took place on the 28th of March, 1999, I believe, in Podujevo where the 211th Armoured Brigade of the Pristina Corps was billeted. One morning the chief of the security of that brigade called me to tell me that in the town of Podujevo itself, corpses were observed. Since I had information that that unit was stationary at that point in time, I ordered that the incident be investigated in full. The information subsequently gathered by the security organs of the Pristina Corps pointed out that a group, a reserve group of the MUP of Serbia arrived on that day early in the morning from the area of Kursumlija or Prolom Banja. Several of them came out of their bus and opened fire on the civilians there. As far as I remember, 12 civilians were killed, including a number of children, I believe. It was ascertained by the security organs of the corps was that the same unit was driven out of Kosovo the same day. I don't know what their fate was from that point on, but I do know that an investigating magistrate from Prokuplje carried out an investigation. He was afraid initially to carry out an on-site investigation, but he eventually did so two days later. I know that as early as 2000, two people were prosecuted in Prokuplje. As far as I could gather from the media later on, the entire group was subsequently prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the status of the document will be changed from MFI to exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 33 it says that there was a reserve group of the MUP, whereas it should be a reserve formation or reserve force of the MUP. Line 23, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could we have the number of that document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one? D210.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'd like to change topics now. Perhaps, Your Honour, this would be a good time for the break so as to resume in continuity when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, are you aware of the term Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you first heard of that term and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first became aware of the term when Colonel Djakovic told me about it. He was then the chief of the operations department in the Pristina Corps Command. Colonel Djakovic told me that there was an internal agreement between him and General Pavkovic to undertake activities in terms of co-ordination concerted action between the VJ and the MUP, and to call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When did Djakovic tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any additional information regarding this co-ordination effort between the army and the MUP? If so, who did you receive it from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information to the effect that the term Joint Command started to be used in late June and particularly throughout July, August, and September 1998. The term was in reference to some joint meetings of the MUP staff for Kosovo and Metohija and representatives of the Pristina Corps Command. At these meetings, co-ordination concerted action were discussed. They would also inform each other about the situation in Kosovo. It was about co-ordination and concerted action vis-a-vis the anti-terrorist activities by the MUP and the VJ in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this the same period when the plan to combat terrorism was implemented in the summer and early autumn 1998?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We were looking at some documents yesterday, and I believe the batch included one my own documents dated the 24th of July, in which I put forward an assessment of the overall security situation in Kosovo and Metohija. I believe that some other technical bodies, such as the state security and political bodies also presented their own assessments. Sometime in late July 1998, the conclusion was reached that the security situation was exceptionally difficult and precarious at the time. For this reason, the plan was to launch an anti-terrorist operation in order to combat terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that this was first implemented, was there a forward command post of the 3rd Army that was set up as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around that time in the month of July, the Pristina Corps Commander realised that the situation along the Albanian border was very difficult. He issued an order to set up a forward command post of the Pristina Corps in the Djakovica garrison. In addition to that, the 3rd Army commander wanted to be able to better monitor the situation in Kosovo, so he also set up a forward command post for the 3rd Army in the Kosovo's heros barracks in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever attend any co-ordination meetings between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps Command, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never attended any such co-ordination meetings. There were other people who were in charge of that, specifically officers from the operative organ of the Pristina Corps Command. As far as I know, normally the Colonel Djakovic would go to these meetings, and sometimes his administrative assistant Lieutenant-Colonel Tesevic was also there. I'm not sure if any other officers were ever there attending these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where these meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be positive about it, nevertheless based on what Colonel Djakovic told me at the time, I seem to remember these meetings being held at the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija. I am not sure if there were any other venues being used for these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your information at these co-ordination meetings, were any decisions ever taken on how to use any units of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No such decisions were ever taken at those meetings because the VJ units had a clear chain of command as far as their operations in Kosovo and Metohija were concerned. And everything was co-ordinated by the 3rd Army Command. The Pristina Corps itself was subordinated to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear that at any point throughout 1999, the chain of command, such as defined by the regulations, was at any point violated, especially during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that. The chain of command continues to operate as envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to these co-ordination meetings in 1998. How long did these meetings go on for, do you perhaps know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The co-ordination meetings between the MUP staff and the Pristina Corps were quite frequent in late July 1998. They continued throughout September and October, all the way up to mid-November, or thereabouts, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you share any information with commander Pavkovic, or did you perhaps receive any information from these co-ordination meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I pointed out yesterday, all the information was being pulled or channelled, all security-related information, into the security section. We kept track of all the locations, manpower, intentions, and ambitions of the KLA, and we also kept track of the problems along the border of the Republic of Albania. On a daily basis Colonel Djakovic wanted me to submit such information to the command organs. They had the information whenever there was an anti-terrorist operation or action in the offing or in progress. As far as I know, Colonel Djakovic would also submit such information to organs of the MUP during their co-ordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout 1999, was the work performed by the security section of the Pristina Corps ever checked or reviewed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the NATO aggression, there were two occasions when the Supreme Command staff sent people there to review the work of the security section, and the security bodies throughout the Pristina Corps as an overall structure. There was General Geza Farkas, one of the security section chiefs. I think I'm talking about early May 1999, that was the first time. And the second time a review was held was between the 1st and the 6th or 7th of June, 1999, and this was performed by the deputy chief of the security administration, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and by the assistant chief of the security administration, General Branko Gajic, and the chief of the security department of the 3rd Army, Colonel Stojadin Antic. Those three men reviewed the work of some security organs and sections in the specified period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During these reviews did General Vasiljevic and the other people who were there for that purpose ever spend any time with the Pristina Corps commander, or indeed with the 3rd Army commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't spend any time with the 3rd Army commander. Nevertheless, General Vasiljevic, and this was the done thing under the military procedures then in place, naturally got in touch with the 3rd Army Command who was at the time in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if General Pavkovic and General Vasiljevic met during that time? If so, when, and how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that throughout their stay, those six days they spent in Kosovo, General Vasiljevic only ever met General Pavkovic once. This occurred at a meeting to which I too was invited. They had invited me to that meeting from the Pristina Corps and the security organs there. General Vasiljevic was there too. They said that he too should be there. At that meeting, General Vasiljevic met General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Prior to this invitation were you aware of the fact that a meeting would be held, or was the invitation sudden and unexpected?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, even earlier on during the war, the scheduling in relation to command meetings was not that specific really. At any rate, I was at my command post, and we would normally carry out routine assessments. Whenever someone, some of the clerks and assistants, for example, would convey an order by General Lazarevic telling us to go to a meeting saying that the 3rd Army commander General Pavkovic would be there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you went to that meeting, did you know what exactly would be on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I expected that as per usual, the commander would want me to brief him on the security situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where you went with General Vasiljevic, and was there anyone else who came with you? I mean, when you were actually on your way to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were on our way to the meeting, there were only General Vasiljevic and I. We went to a room that housed the information centre of the Pristina Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was there when you arrived, and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to the information centre room of the Pristina Corps Command, in addition to a number of officers using the computers there sorting out various records to do with soldiers who were in those units, seated at the table were General Pavkovic, next to him, General Lazarevic, and quite near in a semicircle was the MUP staff commander for Kosovo and Metohija, General Lukic, as well as chief of the state security sector for Kosovo and Metohija, Misa Vilotic. General Vasiljevic exchanged greetings with General Lazarevic and all the other persons present there. Afterwards we simply sat down at the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the date the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe on the 1st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone tell you why the meeting was convened in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we came to that room, I looked at the expressions of those in attendance, and I immediately realised that everyone was somehow taken aback, and everyone was silent, which surprised me. I realised that General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic were quite pale. It was then that General Pavkovic addressed us saying that we were expecting the arrival of Mr. Sainovic who had arrived from Belgrade to brief us on the political situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, can you repeat the name of the person who was in charge of state security in Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the head of the state security sector in Kosovo and Metohija was Mr. Misa Vilotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Save for Generals Pavkovic and Lazarevic, and yourself as well as Mr. Vasiljevic, were there any other representatives of the VJ at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, but later on General Slobodan Kovacevic arrived. He was chief of the administration for tank and armoured units at the Supreme Command staff. He arrived from the field a bit later. I don't think he was familiar with the agenda of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sainovic finally arrive, and what was the actual agenda?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we sat down, there was no discussion. I told you that everyone was silent. Shortly after, Mr. Sainovic entered the room, escorted by the president of the temporary Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija, Mr. Andjelkovic, first name Branislav. They sat down at the same table where Generals Lazarevic and Pavkovic were. As per soldierly protocol, whenever a superior enters or a senior politician, we rise to our feet. We did so and then they sat down next to Lazarevic and Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What was the topic of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole meeting was surprisingly short. It lasted only about quarter of an hour, perhaps 20 minutes. We were addressed by the 3rd Army commander, General Pavkovic. He said that Mr. Sainovic had just arrived from Belgrade wishing to acquaint us with the current political situation and the development during the negotiations process. As far as I recall, by that time there were already talks between the president of the FRY and the representative Trojka concerning the cessation of hostilities in Kosovo in an attempt to come up with a peaceful solution for Kosovo. Next Mr. Sainovic told us that the negotiations between President Milosevic and the representative delegation were nearing their end whereby an agreement would be signed. It was likely that the agreement will entail the withdrawal of the MUP and VJ from Kosovo. Misa Vilotic, the head of the state sector rose. Upon hearing that, he asked what was all about and who signed that, he said: "There's no way I would shake hands with Hashim Thaqi." General Kovacevic, who was sometimes a misfit, and he added something to the effect, and I apologise for my words, We are being screwed, it seems. General Lazarevic said that he had an action underway somewhere in Jablanica, I believe, although I'm uncertain, and General Lukic said that he also had certain activities undergoing at that time. Then Mr. Sainovic told them this: The agreement will be signed, if it hasn't been already. You need to see for yourselves what you will do with those activities. They have to be completed. See what you can do with the competent commands. They have to stop because there would be an agreement followed by the withdrawal of the army and MUP from Kosovo and Metohija. After that information was shared, none of those in attendance said anything. I followed General Vasiljevic out of the room. When Mr. Sainovic addressed me in passing. He said, Colonel, how are the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija going to react to such an agreement? I asked him, or rather, I told him this, Sir, once the first soldier leaves Kosovo and Metohija, you can count on all non-Albanian population leaving Kosovo and Metohija for fear of their safety. Mr. Andjelkovic who otherwise frequently smiled, laughed at that point. I addressed him brusquely, and I told him that this was difficult for me to bear given that I was a soldier and someone who hails from Kosovo. We left the room, and I don't know what followed in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this: Could Mr. Andjelkovic's name be Zoran?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they usually referred to him as Baki, but it could be that his name is Zoran. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you and General Vasiljevic left the room. You left the information centre. Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to the deployment area of the security section of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss the meeting on your way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We discussed some current security issues in Kosovo and Metohija concerning the work of security organs, but we didn't discuss the meeting. It was my impression as if General Vasiljevic had known ahead of time that there would be an agreement signed shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you portions of General Vasiljevic's testimony before this Tribunal in this case. At page 5691 and 5692 of the transcript, he said that he called General Pavkovic and told him that had arrived in Pristina. Pavkovic wanted to see him and invited him to the Pristina Corps Command. Does this correspond to what you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of General Pavkovic speaking to Mr. Vasiljevic, but I explained in detail the only meeting which I attended when I saw of Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Vasiljevic further states that the two of you went to the command of the Pristina Corps and that General Pavkovic said, Stay here, there will be a Joint Command meeting followed by a dinner. Does this tally with what you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely not. Since General Vasiljevic was sitting next to me, I didn't notice him speaking to anyone after the meeting. I don't even know whether under such circumstances any dinner was planned and whether it would have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next General Vasiljevic states that the place where you were was something like an operations room with maps on walls and lots of officers. Does this correspond to the location you remember as the place of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The operations room or an operations room is usually next to the office of the corps commander. The corps commander was deployed in several locations around Pristina changing locations from time to time. And the operations organ was always next to the commander because that person was in charge of suggesting what combat operations would be undertaken. It could be that General Vasiljevic concluded this: There was Colonel Djokic there, who was the assistant commander for mobilisation and personnel affairs, and by nature of his task he is in charge of keeping records of those killed, wounded, and missing among the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, as of the beginning of the war did the operation centre of the Pristina Corps, as well as the command headed by General Lazarevic, move to the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Pristina Corps Command could not be close to the Grand Hotel in tactical terms because it was close to the peacetime corps command building, and it was expected to be targeted at any moment by NATO aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Vasiljevic further says that in addition to Pavkovic and Lazarevic, as well as yourself, there were also MUP generals there: Generals Djordjevic, Stevanovic and Lukic. Does this correspond to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that meeting General Djordjevic was not present, and nor was General Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Before your testimony today, when did you testify before this Tribunal last, and when?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified before this Court in the Milutinovic et al. case. In particular, during the case of General Lazarevic since during the war I was his chief of security section. I don't know whether it was a year or two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This may seem a silly question, but was General Djordjevic on trial at that time when you testified here?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milutinovic was on trial as well as General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, and General Lukic. As well as Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you meet from the Defence team of Mr. Djordjevic and when for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear about your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has his Defence team. My question is this, when did you meet for the first time any of the members of the Defence team of Mr. Djordjevic? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only person I met is you. A month ago you came to Nis where I live with my family. You introduced yourself and asked me if I wanted to testify in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasiljevic goes on to say in this case that as you were returning from the meeting he asked you what this Joint Command is. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no discussion of the so-called Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this portion of the Milutinovic trial took place in closed session. Perhaps Mr. Stamp could give us a hand with that. Ms. O'Leary has drawn my attention to that. Having read all of this, I know that a part of this evidence was presented in closed session. I'm not sure if we should go into closed session for that purpose right now. I'm talking about the 8th of June specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment nothing has appeared which suggests there's any reason for us to be in closed session. I don't know what it is that you propose, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my attention has been drawn to the fact that some of this took place in closed session in the Milutinovic trial. Right now to be perfectly honest, I'm not sure which particular portion. I believe it's my next question, therefore, we might just press on and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever tell Mr. Vasiljevic that you had been sent away from Joint Command meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I possibly have been sent away from these meetings if I never attended one to begin with?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vasiljevic goes on to state you told him that you had been informing General Dimitrijevic about Joint Command meetings. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never informed General Dimitrijevic about Joint Command meetings. As for General Dimitrijevic throughout 1998 while he was chief of the security administration, I may have spoken to him twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm not sure if this should be done in closed session or not because I hear that the question that I'm about to ask was, in fact, asked in closed session. To be perfectly honest, I see no reason for that now, but I think it is up to you, Your Honours, to choose the course of action that I should take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... as to whether something occurred or not occurred, I don't think that requires us to be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, General Vasiljevic appeared as a witness in this trial suggesting you lied when you said that General Djordjevic did not, in fact, attend this meeting. He assumes you changed your statements.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never change my statements. I believe my memory still serves me well, and I still recollect everything that I saw, that I heard in all the meetings I attended. Following my appearance in the Milutinovic trial, I never discussed this with anyone at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I just was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I would just request some page references for these statements of Vasiljevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. The last one was 5930, lines 9 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, would you have any reason to do anything else but to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same thing applies to the present situation as to any other. Throughout my whole life, my job has been to look for the truth. I don't see any reason now, or ever, for me to not do just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone specifically ask you to not tell the truth regarding General Djordjevic's presence at the meeting that took place on the 1st of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such request has been made to me regarding this matter or any other. I can afford to be very categorical about that. I was never asked by anyone to not tell the truth, or indeed, to say something that somebody else wanted me to say. All I'm telling you here is based on my recollection things I saw, things I heard, meetings I myself attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know Nike Peraj?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Captain 1st Class Nike Peraj exceptionally well. I'm also quite well acquainted with his entire family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since when have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nike Peraj, or rather Captain Nike Peraj (redacted) (redacted). I first heard of him when I arrived in Kosovo and Metohija to serve there back in 1993 [Realtime translation read in error "1998"]. Later on, I was in a position to contact him many times over some quite specific matters to do with the work of the (redacted). The tasks that Mr. Peraj was performing required the presence of an experienced operative, some of the tasks, that is. Given the fact that I was chief, and given the fact that that was the MO established by my predecessors as chiefs in the security section of the Pristina Corps. I can state with certainty from what time on exactly Captain 1st Class Nike Peraj (redacted) (redacted), regardless of that, it certainly applied throughout this entire time. The time I met him back in 1993 and 1999 when the army withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija. I'm saying throughout this time, (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You pause, Mr. Djurdjic. First, the transcript page 43, line 3 has 1998. I believe the witness said 1993. Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I think that this material has been covered in private session before, so if we are discussing it, we should be in private session, and if this part of the transcript could be made private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, that raises the question of what was the reason for the earlier private session because at the moment, nothing occurs to me that requires this evidence to be in private session. Is there something that you could assist me with? Mr. Stamp, I see you volunteering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was just making -- well, referring to my own memory. I believe that the evidence in respect to

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: (redacted) was taken in private session both in this case and in the prior case, in the Milutinovic case. There were some sensitive issues in respect to what his role was and what he was doing, and private session had been requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the moment then, based on what you recall, we will redact references to Captain Peraj (redacted) (redacted). There are, I think, two or three such references in the transcript. And we will revisit that if necessary at some later time. But out of caution, we will redact that now. While we are dealing with that subject and before it goes off the screen, we seem to have the dates 1993, 1999, and 1998 somewhat confusingly in the record. I think 1998 may have been an error because it was in the context of when this witness first met Captain Peraj, and I think you said that was 1993. And is the end of the captain's service that you are speaking about in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the end of the captain's service and also what we were meant to discuss in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's just confirming that area. Now, do you have further questions about this subject? Are they going to require closed session in view of the ruling or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I propose that we avoid using the person's name. As far as I understand, the transcript will show what it shows, and we will all know who we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, for professional reasons, I would like to ask you to perhaps choose the option of going into closed session. There might be consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think the practical way forward at the moment is to hear evidence on this subject from now on in closed session. At the moment it's not clear why that is necessary, but as we heard evidence earlier in closed session and in view of what has just been suggested by the witness, we think the safer course is to hear the evidence out in closed session. We may have reason later to reconsider whether there was any necessity for this in light of what it is that may emerge, but for the moment out of precaution we will deal with the matter in closed session. Closed session. For practical reasons we will go into private session rather than closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We've run some checks during the break and we now know that when the statement of this witness was discussed in the Milutinovic case, the witness that we mentioned, it was actually done in open session, not in closed session.
