That is regarding Mr. Stamp's earlier attempts to shed light on the matter. Therefore, I assume that we may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, when did you find out about the operation in the Carragojs valley?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about the operation in the Carragojs valley on the 27th, the morning of the 27th, as a matter of fact. The subordinate security chiefs were under an obligation to report to me on the situation in their own areas of responsibility each morning and each evening. This included any operations being performed by the army. I specifically learned about this on the 28th. And then after that each of the security organs were duty-bound to submit a written report on the progress of the operation. This was then collated with the telegrams that were coming in and a single document was then drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us leave the operation aside for a moment. When one commences an operation, an operation that is planned, how exactly do the security organs keep the Pristina Corps Command informed? What is the substance of the information that you are likely to receive in a situation like that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the commencement of an operation, the security organs would normally report that on such and such a day, such and such an operation is planned, the objective being this or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What if there's nothing extraordinary or out of the ordinary happening during an operation that warrants reporting to the Pristina Corps? What were the reports you received like in situations such as described?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such situations, I received no reports at all. One thing is certain, however, any time an operation is completed, I must get a report, an oral report, followed by a written report detailing aspects such as which operation was launched and completed, how it was implemented, and whether the security organs came across any problems during the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now go back to the specific situation -- operation that we were talking about. When exactly did you receive a report following the completion of the Carragojs valley operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communications equipment was used to forward to me an oral report on the 28th, and then depending on how soon my mail got there normally within two or three days, I would be receiving a written report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Following the operation in the Carragojs valley, was there any indication of any unusual or extraordinary circumstances that arose during the operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the reports I received on this operation my assistant for staff and security affairs who at the same time was responsible for technical guidance of the military police, the only piece of information I received was that a soldier, a military policemen specifically, was killed during that operation. That was the only thing that stood out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where were you on the 27th of April 1999 and on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I will now be showing you portions of witness Peraj's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P313. Exhibit P313.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask you this, paragraph 6 of the statement in which the witness states that Colonel Dosan was responsible for the VJ units across Djakovica municipality for the MUP, specifically the reserve unit, and that the VJ Corps staff was receiving orders from the defence ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we blow the image up a little, please. Colonel Dosan was only responsible for the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade of which he was commander. What was your other question, sir, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The witness goes on to state that he was also responsible for the MUP and the reserve units.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither Colonel Dosan nor any other commander from the Pristina Corps Command were ever responsible for the MUP. He was the brigade commander and at the same time the commander of the Djakovica garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Finally, the witness says that the VJ Corps staff was receiving orders from the defence ministry in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely untrue. That would have violated the subordination principle. The corps is the third-ranking unit under the defence ministry. It is not an operative unit that receives an order from the defence ministry. It's the Chief of General Staff that receives it, and then he goes through the 3rd Army on to the Pristina Corps Command, and the Pristina Corps Command forwards this down to their own units including the 52nd Brigade of which Dosan was commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: What about the defence ministry in Belgrade, does it issue any orders to the VJ General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence ministry is a technical body, but there was actually the Supreme Command staff at the period under consideration, and in terms of operative command over the army, this was the relevant body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not sure you understand what I'm asking you. We are talking about war time circumstances now, okay, Supreme Command staff, but what about the defence ministry, the defence ministry of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Who was the defence minister during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. The defence minister had the power to issue orders to the VJ General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A what about the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, there is one thing, the Supreme Defence Council is a supreme body in terms of running the VJ. There were the presidents in that council of both the republics, Serbia and Montenegro, as well as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and then it had some additional members such as the defence minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He would have attending meetings as would any other persons actually invited by the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who had the right to make decisions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The three presidents that you mentioned as members of that body, right, is that who you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's who I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how then could the defence minister possibly have issued any orders to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command or rather the Supreme Command staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council had the power to issue orders to the staff and then the staff would then send the orders down the chain of command to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then the defence ministry is what?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A technical body, it's a technical body dealing with problems within the defence ministry, such as the budget, such as supplies and equipment, but the Supreme Defence Council was the body that actually had the power to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 8, please. I think we are on the right page of the English. The witness says that he left the VJ three days before KFOR arrived in Kosovo. He had learned from a source in Montenegro that the Serbian military court in Nis had sentenced him and another five VJ soldiers to 15 years imprisonment for desertion.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said awhile ago, when he left the army -- well, actually, the army first left Kosovo and Metohija and then after that KFOR arrived which happened over a number of stages. As for the other thing, I actually don't know about that. Nevertheless, I believe I can say that this person was never convicted by any court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 20 goes on to state that between February and March numerous volunteers joined, mostly from Russia. Does that ring a bell? Did such a thing occur, as a matter of fact, in February or March? Were there any volunteers before the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were none before the war. The first volunteers started arriving in April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further down in paragraph 21 we see this: The witness claims that Frenki's units were reservists of the VJ for awhile. Can we just go back to the previous page. I think you can see the beginning of that paragraph now, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, as a matter of fact, but I believe I can answer straightaway. Frenki's men, I think the gentleman is here referring to the special operations units and they were never VJ reservists nor were they ever an organic component of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were they a paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular unit under the authority of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In para 23, the witness says that the RS Brigade of about 1.000 personnel arrived before the NATO bombing and that it was deployed to Rezina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, this is definitely untrue. No unit of Republika Srpska was present in Kosovo and Metohija during that period. How is it possible for a brigade to March from Republika Srpska down to Kosovo under NATO bombardment? It would be crazy to plan something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for any unit to enter Kosovo and Metohija especially the size of a brigade, and that you, as the chief of the security section, would be ignorant of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, especially not a unit such an armoured vehicle brigade. Such a brigade usually has about 250 tanks, armoured personnel carriers or other types of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Further down in para 25 the witness says that that brigade was in the Djakovica area and that his unit provided logistical support?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a brigade was never in the area of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the next page in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The witness says that concerning the collection of information and reports from the different commanders in the field, Colonel Kotur was in charge of that at the staff level. He forwarded that information to the VJ general Colonel Dusan Samardzic. From Nis that information was sent on to the minister of defence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely untrue. Colonel not Branko but Milan Kotur was one of the officers from the command of the Pristina Corps who was at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps Command in Djakovica. In terms of establishment, he was the chief of infantry in the Pristina Corps. This type of reporting could not have existed. Colonel Kotur could have reported to the forward command post in Djakovica and then the forward command post could pass information on to the Pristina Corps Command. Also, he was never in charge of collecting information as is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about this part where it says that the 3rd Corps Command passed information on to the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably had in mind the command of the 3rd Army. The 3rd Army Command could only have sent information to the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 40. The witness states that in the area of Djakovica, there were 200 members of paramilitary units, mostly Arkan's and Seselj's men, whereas there were some 30 of Frenki's men.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous case I testified, I said that in the area of Kosovo and Metohija there were no Arkan's units nowhere including Djakovica. As for any of Frenki's men, as he calls them, that was a JSO unit. They were not in Djakovica, they were in Decani, above the monastery in Visoki, Decani, not in the town of Decani itself. There were only active-duty soldiers and conscripts who had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 57, the witness states that you were his good friend and that in early 1999 you mentioned to him a plan of ethnic cleansing that the Serbian forces would carry out against the Kosovo Albanian population in the municipality of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim in full responsibility that the term "ethnic cleansing" is alien to me. I have never said such a thing to anyone, including this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In para 59, the witness says that in April 1999 after an attack Milutin Prascevic was killed in an ambush set up by the KLA. He also says that he attended a meeting in a private home in Djakovica near the barracks attended by the chief of the state security Sreto Camovic, a MUP corporal by the name of Kovacevic, Captain Sergej Perovic, an officer from the security of the 69th Air-borne Brigade, and yourself. And that during that meeting, you apparently said to Micunovic and Kovacevic, or rather ordered them to execute an operation in the Carragojs valley in retaliate for Prascevic's murder and that on that occasion at least one hundred people were supposed to be killed and all houses set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having testified before and in the course of this testimony, I had occasion to go through the entire statement of this witness. It is my position that it is full of untruths and lies. This entire paragraph, for instance. First of all, Milutin Prascevic was not a MUP officer, he was a civilian working in the MUP in Djakovica. Secondly, such a meeting was never held. Third, some people he refers to such as Kovacevic, I have never met or seen that person. I have only heard of him as being a chief of SUP in Djakovica for awhile. Lastly, such a meeting was never held, and I have never said something of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 62, the witness states that he attended a meeting when the massacre in Meja was planned. This was in the same building where he had been stationed in with his unit, where he was in charge of security. Apparently you saw him on that occasion and greeted him, and you took him as one of his soldiers. He also states that at that meeting, the massacre in Meja was planned.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For umpteenth time, I must say the following: In terms of my functional duty, I was in no position to plan any activities. I did not have that authority. It was not in my job description. I could not have ordered such an action. I was not at this meeting, and this is a pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In para 65, the witness states that the operation was headed by Goran Jeftovic, a staff officer of the Pristina Corps in charge of operations.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation in Meja was not led by Lazarevic because he was not in Djakovica at the time. Jeftovic was not in charge either because Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftovic was one of the officers at the forward command post who was in charge of providing security and guard service for the command post. The operation was led by the forward command post headed by commander, Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps Colonel Veroljub Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 95, the witness states that Milos Dosan did not approve the operations in Korenica and Meja, he did not approve of it, that's why he had Micunovic arrested for his participation. However, Micunovic remained behind bars for only three days.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Dosan as brigade commander could not have either approved, approved of, or dispute the action. He was only another unit commander of which there were several. Such an action could have only been planned and ordered by the forward command post. This piece of information stating that Colonel Dosan had Micunovic arrested is a lie. Neither was Micunovic subordinated to Colonel Kotur, nor could Colonel Kotur have anyone arrested. There were organs in charge of that. He could have informed the military police or those competent to do so. Brigade commanders do not arrest other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Had there been an arrest, would you as the chief of security section of Pristina Corps have been informed of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I would have been informed of any arrest, orally and by written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 96, the witness goes on to say that in Lazarevic's office there was a map in clear talc covering an entire wall. Jeftovic was marking the map in details about the operation occurring in the Carragojs valley. He says that the data indicated on the map tallied with what he could see in the field.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, there is a procedure indicating who is allowed to enter the operations room in terms of title or function, even certain senior officers had no access to it, and especially not a mere captain 1st class such as Nike Peraj. Secondly, at the forward command post there was a working map, but it was a general map kept daily indicating terrorist locations and border incidents. I don't think that the Meja action map was ever put on a wall. Also, this witness, by the way, did not complete any military schooling. How could he have interpreted that map and get his bearings on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 97, there the witness states that in conversations with you and Perovic during 1998 and in early 1999, as well as from operational briefings he attended in Djakovica and Pristina, and based on operational maps presented in these briefings, he became aware of the general military plan for the Djakovica area.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, such conversations never took place. Secondly, there were no plans prepared ahead of time for any area including the Djakovica area. The only thing that existed were plans of disposition of our units and terrorist positions. On such documents one could also see where our border posts were located as well as our forces in the border area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, the 72nd Special Brigade, whose brigade was it and what kind of a brigade was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there were two elite units. One was the 63rd Air-borne Brigade and the other was the 73rd Special Brigade commanded by the Special Forces corps. And then in turn under direct General Staff command, the 73rd Special Brigade also had under it an anti-terrorist battalion as well as a scouting sabotage battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was this brigade or any of its part in 1999 in Kosovo and Metohija during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly when. The whole brigade was not there, only the anti-terrorist battalion of the 72nd Special Brigade was there since it was resubordinated to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded the anti-terrorist battalion, I think that's what you called it, yes, of the 72nd Special Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion was commanded directly by the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the commander of that 72nd Special Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Jovanovic. I may have gotten the last name wrong, but I can't quite remember. The name escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to keep track of all the names, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I got lost between the 73rd and the 72nd. Are they two distinct units? One is said to be the 73rd Special Brigade as appears at the end of page 62 beginning of page 63. And then at 63, line 7 and a bit later we hear of the 72nd Special Brigade. I think the context says they are referring to what earlier was said to be the 73rd Special Brigade, is that correct, or is there something I have missed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is the 72nd Special Brigade. And that is the unit that the witness is discussing. And the other special unit in the VJ was the 63rd Parachuter's Brigade. The 72nd is the special Brigade. The 73rd is an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but what we have here just about to go off the screen is two references to the 73rd Special Brigade. Now, is that incorrect? Perhaps the witness can tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 72nd Special Brigade. The 63rd Parachuter's Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The references to 73rd Brigade at the end of page 63 beginning of 64 should be to the 72nd Special Brigade. Then at line 12 we have mention of the 72nd Special Battalion. Should that be the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have been speaking too fast. Everything you've just said is perfectly correct. Just that it's not the 72nd Special Battalion. It's the anti-terrorist battalion which is part of the 72nd Special Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Your Honour, for clarifying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Another thing that I want to ask you, General, sir, let me ask you this again. I've asked you this a number of times already. Was there any unit of the Pristina Corps that was actually under your command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat this, but if you go to any military documents or archives this should be easy enough to check, not a single unit was under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you now what Witness K-73 said. You were told who the witness was during proofing, right? In order to protect the person's identity, we shall not be using the person's name. This is Exhibit P330. That's his statement. There is something in particular that I'd like to point out to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try 330A, in that case. That one is not under seal. I don't think that should pose a problem then. This should be page 7 in the B/C/S. Just a minute, please. Can we have the previous page back in the English because it's the beginning of the document that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 33, the witness says that at the time the 72nd Special Brigade and his own anti-terrorist detachment would be under the command of Colonel Momir Stojanovic chief of security in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This witness's statement is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. He goes on to state as follows: "Three weeks after our arrival in Nasec we received orders from Colonel Stojanovic to ambush vehicles at a crossroads near Nasec no matter if there were Albanians or Serbs in those vehicles?"

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to orders by the corps commander I was given a task. Officially I was on my way to the Prizren garrison. The commander also knew that I was a native of Kosovo and that I was familiar with the area. My task was to take that battalion away, to March it away from there and take it to a children's resort, an abandoned one, on the banks of the Drim river, so that's what I did. I took that battalion away. I marched it out of the area. And I didn't stay for any time at all. I did not receive any orders then or ever to that battalion, nor indeed did I have the power to do that. As far as I know the battalion was used for in-depth securing activities of the state border near Mount Pastrik where the border offices could no longer withstand attacks by the terrorists. Pastrik on the border post of Kosare were the two points where the greatest pressure was being exerted by the terrorists. Later during the NATO air-strikes there was an attempt at breaking through there in order to create two corridors to allow two large groups of terrorists to get in and link up with those inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, who was the commander of the 52nd Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Stevo Kopanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about A-73's rank?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A-73, well, first of all, I never saw that witness. He was there as a soldier on a contract and then he was an active soldier after which I believe he held the rank of lance corporal. Nevertheless, don't take this at face value, simply because I am not sure. I do apologise, just one thing. I do happen to know his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please no names.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand that. He was an active duty captain working with a reconnaissance company. I spoke to his father, that being the only reason I know who this person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is K-73. Not A-73. Just for the transcript. That is the witness we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My next question: Can a squad commander attend meetings held by the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules on the work of VJ staffs clearly state that. They state the terms for such meetings, and I think the units in Kosovo fully complied with that. Only the direct subordinates to the battalion commander can do that, in this case, company commanders and independent platoon commanders only if there were any independent platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 40 of the witness's statement says that while they were still in Junik, Commander Kopanja convened all of the officers and instructed them to start cleaning up the area from the Albanians who were there. He clearly said that all the Albanian civilians should be sent towards Korenica where the MUP people would be waiting for them with a list of names indicating who the terrorists were.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very much doubt the accuracy of this particular portion of the witness's statement. First of all, how can Kopanja possibly know ahead of time that there is an operation being planned for a certain area? I don't think even higher ranking officers had access to that kind of information. He was a battalion commander in charge of something altogether different. Secondly, there were exceptionally honourable officers working in these military police units. When these positions were awarded to them, all of them were previously vetted. I simply can't believe that the commander of this unit could ever have stated anything like that simply because he would have been altogether unfamiliar with any plans to do with the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the commander of the 52nd Military Police Battalion was stationed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command and by virtue of that fact the commander of the 52nd Military Police Battalion throughout the NATO aggression were stationed in the general Pristina city area. All of the elements of the Pristina Corps Command, which was his primary duty, the security of those elements, I mean, were, in fact, within the general Pristina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Just in case you remember, was the 52nd Military Police Battalion in April 1999 in Junik in its entirety including all its elements?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this never happened throughout the war. The battalion was never whole in a single piece as it were because of the nature of their duties and business. As far as the 52nd Military Police Battalion is concerned, only two of its platoon were at one point resubordinated to the 152nd Military Police Company [as interpreted] which itself was part of the 125th Motorised Brigade whose focus was on the Junik mountains and the General Kosare area engaged in bloody battles with the terrorist, suffering over 100 casualties and deaths. This 125th Military Police Company before these two platoons were sent there and resubordinated had been decimated. The company commander had been wounded. Two other commanders had been killed. There were other soldiers who had been killed, therefore the corps commander, in order to raise their morale and in order to strengthen the company, that those two platoons be resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something that I've noticed, page 68, line 10, reads the 152nd Military Police Company. It should be the 52nd. Now here it reads 125th Motorised Brigade whereas you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 125th Military Police Company that was part of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The 125th company's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One speaker at a time, please. Repeat both the question and the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you will notice that the previous question and answer were not interpreted because you and the witness were overlapping. You'll have to go over it again if you think it important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, two platoons, of the 52nd Battalion of the military police, who were these resubordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two platoons were resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade and now became part of the 125th Military Police Company which itself was part of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was the direct immediate superior to the commanders of these platoons that were resubordinated to the 125th Military Police Company that was itself part of the 125th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their immediate superior was the commander of the 125th Military Police Company, and his superior was the commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you very much for your evidence, sir. Thank you very much, Your Honours, for bearing with me and allowing me to complete my examination. No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Clearly with a minute to go we will need to adjourn. We continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I am afraid this has taken longer than expected, so we must ask you to return again tomorrow. A Court Officer will assist you out. We now adjourn to resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.
